title: Calling an AI Agent Your 'Coworker' Backfires
hook: Companies are giving AI agents names and org-chart spots like real employees. Research says that framing makes people worse at their jobs — catching fewer errors and dodging responsibility.
key_points: Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google all market AI agent tools as digital colleagues.
Nearly a third of managers say their company already treats AI agents as employees.
A Boston University study found framing a tool as a 'coworker' cut error-catching by 18%.
The same framing made people 44% more likely to defer mistakes to a manager instead of fixing them.
MIT Tech Review's takeaway: honest 'this is software' framing beats flattering anthropomorphism.
content_html: Some companies now give their AI agents names, job titles, and even a spot on the org chart — Nvidia's CEO has described workplaces full of "digital humans" going through onboarding. MIT Technology Review reports that Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have all shipped tools for managing teams of AI agents, marketed as digital colleagues, and that nearly a third of surveyed managers say their company already frames its AI agents as employees.
extra_html: The framing isn't harmless. The article cites Boston University researcher Emma Wiles, whose study found that presenting an AI tool as a "coworker" — rather than plainly as software — made people catch 18% fewer of its errors, and made them 44% more likely to punt a mistake up to a manager instead of correcting it themselves. In other words, dressing up a tool as a colleague seems to make people trust it more and supervise it less — exactly backward from what a genuinely useful tool needs. The piece's argument is straightforward: an agent named "Alex" is still software, and pretending otherwise doesn't make it smarter, it just makes the humans around it more careless. Honest framing — this helps, but you're still responsible for checking it — is the boring advice that actually holds up.

related.title: AI Agents: AI That Does Things
related.hook: A chatbot answers; an agent acts. The new frontier is AI that can browse, click, book, and complete multi-step tasks for you — powerful, and exactly why you keep it on a leash.

related.title: Over-Relying on AI
related.hook: The subtle risk isn't that AI fails — it's that it usually works, so you stop checking. Trusting a confident machine over your own judgment is its own kind of mistake.

related.title: AI at Work
related.hook: The biggest everyday payoff from AI is at work: drafting the email, summarizing the meeting, untangling the spreadsheet formula. The trick is using it without leaking secrets or trust.

flashcards.prompt: What did the Boston University study find about calling an AI tool a 'coworker'?

choices.text: People caught 18% fewer errors and were 44% more likely to punt mistakes to a manager
People became 18% more careful and caught every error
It had no measurable effect on behavior
People stopped using the tool entirely

flashcards.explanation_html: Framing an AI tool as a coworker measurably changed behavior for the worse: fewer caught errors and more deferred accountability, per the study cited.

flashcards.prompt: Why does calling an AI agent an 'employee' matter beyond just branding?
flashcards.back_html: It changes how people treat its mistakes — trusting it more like a person and taking less personal responsibility for catching what it gets wrong.
